summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices in Brunei describes the provision as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing were among those enforced under the code at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. That trans-specific offence appears in only nine of the countries that criminalise gender expression, against at least 67 countries that criminalise same-sex relations. A state-sharia analogue exists in Malaysia.

Stage three of the Syariah Penal Code took effect on 3 April 2019 under the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, which was brought into force in stages. It provides for death by stoning for anal sex, adultery and abortion, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex. Homosexuality was already an offence carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment under the previous law. The 2017 State Department report separately records that 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented.

The code applies chiefly to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of an estimated population of 420,000 to 450,000. First-person reporting published as the penalties took effect describes anonymous accounts of a climate of fear and no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.

The sultan stated that Brunei's capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia provisions. The country has carried out no execution since 1957, and a freshness check dated 27 September 2026 found the law still in force with the 2019 moratorium intact. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Brunei to halt the code, Human Rights Watch described it as barbaric, and the United Nations and foreign governments condemned it.

The 2017 State Department report also records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services.
tangentialFactors:
Brunei sits in a small group of jurisdictions: Human Rights Watch identifies at least two states, Brunei and Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise posing as or imitating a person of a different sex, with a comparable provision operating through state sharia in Malaysia. Of the at least 67 countries that criminalise same-sex relations, only nine criminalise gender expression in statute, which places Brunei's Section 198 among the narrower set of trans-specific offences worldwide.

International reaction to stage three was sharp and public. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called for the law to be halted, Human Rights Watch labelled it barbaric, and the United Nations together with foreign governments issued condemnations as the penalties took effect on 3 April 2019.

The enforcement picture is not uniform on its face. Brunei has not carried out an execution since 1957, the sultan has said the moratorium extends to the stoning provisions, and reporting from April 2019 records uncertainty about how far the code would be applied to foreigners. A freshness check on 27 September 2026 found the code still in force and the moratorium undisturbed.

The wider criminal framework already reached same-sex conduct before stage three, with homosexuality punishable by up to 10 years, so the 2019 additions extended penalties rather than creating the underlying prohibition.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same Section 198 wording as visitors, but the code's heaviest provisions apply chiefly to Muslims, about two-thirds of the population of roughly 420,000 to 450,000. Lesbian sex exposes women to 40 strokes of the cane, anal sex and adultery to stoning, and theft to amputation, alongside the pre-existing 10-year maximum for homosexuality.

Local LGBTI people report structural disadvantage as well as penal exposure. The US State Department's 2017 documentation records discrimination experienced by LGBTI people in employment, housing, recreation and services, and notes that morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating and religious propagation were being enforced while the sharia implementing regulations remained unissued.

Reporting published as stage three commenced describes residents speaking anonymously about a climate of fear, and surveys of LGBTI law place Brunei among the small number of states with an express statutory ban on cross-dressing or imitation of the other sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
Four sources in the inventory could not be retrieved at research time and returned HTTP 403: the Norwegian government's hosted copy of Brunei's Penal Code including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, the Human Dignity Trust's April 2019 briefing on implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, a France24 report of April 2019 on fear among Brunei's gay community, and an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. Their specific claims remain unresolved against the primary text.

No source in the inventory reports a conviction under Section 198 after 2017; the only conviction figure available is the US State Department's "no known convictions" finding for 2017, and whether that position has since changed is unresolved.

Whether the sharia implementing regulations that were unissued in 2017 have since been made is not sourced here, and no source addresses legal gender recognition, the text or marker on identity and travel documents, visa or border screening that could expose a visitor's gender history, bathroom or facility rules, access to transition-related healthcare, or recognition of partners or marriages. These gaps are not findings of permissiveness.

Population estimates differ between sources, with 420,000 and 450,000 both appearing in the inventory, and the Muslim share is given as roughly two-thirds.
